transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-02
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 68 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Redwood Infra), Samir Patel (DataWave CTO), Aisha Mohammed (DataWave ML Infra Lead), Liam O'Connor (DataWave SRE), Rosa Kim (DataWave ML Eng)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive to validate profiling methodology and to compare runtime tradeoffs between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM on GPU, with a focus on kernel selection, CUDA Graphs benefits, KV cache behavior, batching patterns, and quantization impact. Customer is interested in private deployment options (VPC / on-prem) and needs concrete numbers for latency/throughput SLOs.

Topics covered:
- Profiling approach (nvprof / Nsight / CUPTI traces, CUDA graphs capture)
- Kernel selection and fused attention kernels (TensorRT-LLM observations)
- vLLM batching and KV cache strategies
- CUDA Graphs to reduce CPU overhead and repeated kernel launch costs
- Quantization tradeoffs (FP16, INT8, GPTQ/AWQ) for generation quality vs throughput
- VPC/on-prem constraints (NCCL vs TCP, KMS/HSM, private registry)

Action items reviewed at end of call (see metadata for owners/dates).

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Thanks everyone for joining. The goal today is a hands-on profiling discussion - Diego from our infra team will run through what we saw when comparing TensorRT-LLM and vLLM on A100/H100 setups and what to expect for CUDA graphs and kernel selection.
[00:18] Samir: Thanks, yeah we want numbers we can show to the infra team. Typical generation is mixed - a lot of 512 token prompts but 95th hits 2k for some workflows. We care about p99 latency under 300ms for small assistant queries and throughput for batch job reranking.
[00:35] Diego: Got it. Quick orientation: we profiled using A100 80GB and H100 80GB, seq lengths 512 and 2048, batch sizes from 1 up to 16 for interactive and 32+ for bulk. Tools: Nsight Systems for timeline + CUPTI for kernel timings, and we recorded CUDA graphs capture to measure kernel launch overhead removal.
[00:57] Aisha: Quick question - when you say CUDA graphs capture, is that something you do at compile time or runtime? We have dynamic prompt lengths so curious how you handle graph re-use.
[01:10] Diego: Good point. We capture a set of graphs keyed by sequence length and batch shape. In practice we use a small set of canonical graphs (e.g., 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048). For lengths in between we fall back to the nearest graph or fall back to the JIT kernel path. There's a tradeoff: more graphs equals more memory and load-time overhead, but fewer graphs increases fallback runtimes.
[01:34] Rosa: Do you see big differences between A100 and H100 with graphs?
[01:37] Diego: H100 gives better tensor cores and yields better INT8/F16 performance; with CUDA graphs the win is mostly reduced CPU overhead so we see slightly better p50/p95 on H100. But kernel selection matters: TensorRT-LLM picks fused attention kernels that can be very efficient for certain shapes, vLLM's kernel set is more generic and sometimes yields better throughput at high batch sizes due to batching heuristics.
[02:05] Samir: Can you expand on the fused kernels? I saw mention of fused attention vs native cuBLAS runs.
[02:13] Diego: Sure - TensorRT-LLM often uses fused-MHA kernels that combine QKV projection + attention + softmax + output projection in fewer kernels. That reduces global memory IO and kernel launch counts. The downside: they're highly shape-specific and don't cover all model variants or custom ops. If your sequence shapes align, TensorRT-LLM can cut kernel time by 20-40% for attention-heavy workloads.
[02:38] Priya: Does Redwood's runtime automatically pick between TensorRT and other kernels?
[02:43] Diego: Our runtime has a kernel-selection layer - during model onboarding we profile common sequence shapes and the runtime chooses a kernel plan: prefer fused kernels when stable and supported, otherwise use fallback kernels. We also consider quantization profile; some fused kernels don't support INT8 or certain QRNN-like ops, so we pick the right path.
[02:59] Liam: For KV cache behavior - we run a lot of multi-turn chat. How does KV caching interact with CUDA graphs?
[03:06] Diego: KV cache is mostly about memory layout and reuse of past keys/values. CUDA graphs help by reducing the per-step kernel launch overhead, but you still pay for memory copies if you aren't careful. Redwood's serving runtime manages a contiguous KV layout per session which reduces scatter/gather. There's also an optimization for prefix caching where we reuse cached tensors as inputs to the graph and only run the incremental steps.
[03:30] Aisha: Any numbers you can share from the profiling runs? p50/p95 for seq512/batch1, seq2048/batch4 etc?
[03:37] Diego: Sure - rough numbers from our test model (7B-ish open model) on H100:
- seq=512, batch=1: TensorRT-LLM median token latency ~9ms, p95 ~18ms. vLLM median ~11ms, p95 ~22ms.
- seq=2048, batch=1: TensorRT-LLM median ~28ms, p95 ~55ms. vLLM median ~33ms, p95 ~65ms.
- seq=512, batch=8 (interactive batching): TensorRT-LLM throughput ~380 tokens/s, vLLM ~340 tokens/s.
- seq=2048, batch=16 (bulk): vLLM's batching heuristics sometimes win because of better packing; throughput ~1.6x of single.
Numbers have noise; we provided raw traces in the sheet.
[04:34] Samir: Interesting. Sounds like TensorRT-LLM wins for single-session low-batch latency, vLLM can win when you aggressively pack requests.
[04:41] Diego: That's a fair summary. Also remember model variants and custom ops can flip that. For example, quantized runs (INT8/GPTQ) on TensorRT often get a big boost IF the kernel supports it and calibration is good. Some fused kernels don't have stable INT8 paths yet so vLLM with its more modular kernels may be easier to quantize.
[05:02] Rosa: You mentioned calibration. We run AWQ/GPTQ for smaller models - does Redwood handle that?
[05:08] Priya: We support GPTQ/AWQ-style quant artifacts in our private deployments; the runtime can load quantized weights and choose appropriate kernels. Diego can add the notes and caveats about which kernels we tested with INT8.
[05:20] Diego: I'll add a table in the sheet. In our runs GPTQ gave roughly 1.5-2x speedup vs FP16 for medium models on H100 in our tests, with ~small quality delta depending on dataset. AWQ had slightly better perf at the cost of more tooling fragility.
[05:36] Samir: Regarding on-prem and VPC - we have strict KMS requirements and can't have egress for model weights. How does Redwood handle private deployments?
[05:45] Maya: We offer Private deployments with a customer-managed control plane; weights can be stored in your private registry and deployed in a VPC. KMS/HSM integration is supported for encryption at rest and for key wrapping. We also have audit logs and RBAC. Diego can follow up with the security doc link.
[05:58] Liam: Network wise, will NCCL be required for multi-GPU? We have limited IB (InfiniBand) in some datacenters.
[06:04] Diego: NCCL/UCX is preferred for multi-GPU high-throughput setups. For single-node multi-GPU we can use NVLink/NCCL. If IB isn't present then TCP+NCCL or CPU fallback will work but expect reduced multi-node perf. We'll outline recommended infra in the next doc.
[06:19] Aisha: On batching - do you do continuous batching like vLLM or time-window batching? We need predictable latency.
[06:27] Diego: Our runtime supports both. There's continuous batching for throughput-first workloads; it packs as requests arrive up to a max latency window. We also support a strict SLO mode where each request is prioritized and we fall back to dedicated capacity or smaller batch sizes. You can set per-route SLOs which triggers routing policies.
[06:43] Samir: For kernel selection heuristics - is it deterministic? For example can we reproduce a perf regression when switching model versions?
[06:50] Diego: We record kernel plans per model version and can lock a plan to make rollouts deterministic. During onboarding we run a profiling sweep and store candidate plans. We also produce an eval suite that replays prompts to detect regressions.
[07:04] Rosa: Any gotchas with CUDA Graphs and dynamic shapes? Earlier you said graph per-length - but what about models with prompt engineering where prefix grows during the session?
[07:14] Diego: For prefix growth we have two approaches: incremental graph execution (where the graph covers the incremental step only) and hybrid graphs+JIT where long prefixes use cached tensors and we only run small-step graphs. It's not perfect; extreme variability makes full graph coverage impractical.
[07:30] Aisha: We run a mix of short and long. Sounds like the hybrid approach is what we want.
[07:35] Diego: Agreed. Also note memory fragmentation can be worse with many graph variants - we recommend tuning the graph set to match your traffic distribution.
[07:45] Samir: Anything else about kernel selection? Compiler flags, cuBLAS versions, or TensorRT versions that change behavior?
[07:52] Diego: Yes - TensorRT and driver versions matter. Some fused kernels were added in TRT 8.x and improved in 9.x; CUDA 12.x and newer NV driver improvements affect kernel timings. We list exact versions in the sheet. Small driver bumps can change perf by 5-10% in some cases.
[08:10] Priya: Will you share the raw traces?
[08:12] Diego: Yep, I'll upload the Nsight timelines, CUPTI kernel tables, and the captured CUDA graphs. Expect links in the benchmark sheet.
[08:19] Maya: OK let's go quickly through next steps: we'll share the sheet, customer to give prompt set and target SLOs, and we schedule the on-prem pilot. Any final Qs?
[08:28] Samir: No, that's it. Appreciate the depth.
[08:31] Maya: Great, thanks all - we'll follow up with action items.

End of transcript.
